glossary.definition: The trace impurity (often manganese, lead, or a rare-earth element) that causes a mineral to fluoresce under UV.
A brilliant, diamond-like shine — the brightest mineral luster. Diamond and cerussite show it.
A soft, billowy blue or white glow that floats across a stone as you turn it. Moonstone is the classic example.
A NWS alert for conditions that are inconvenient or hazardous but not immediately life-threatening.
A measure of pollutants in the air, often reported as an AQI index. Smoke from wildfires can make it dangerous to be outdoors.
An extinct, coiled-shell marine animal related to squid. Their fossils are common and often iridescent.
A crystal with no visible faces — it grew crowded against other minerals and couldn't form its ideal shape.
The ring-shaped zone around each magnetic pole where aurora most commonly appears. It expands equatorward during storms.
A dark, fine-grained volcanic rock — the most common volcanic rock on Earth. Forms much of the ocean floor.
When a crystal splits light into two rays, making a double image through it. Calcite shows this strongly.
A surface shaped like a bunch of grapes — rounded, bubbly mounds. Common in hematite, malachite, and goethite.
A bow-shaped radar signature of a line of damaging thunderstorms. Often produces straight-line winds and occasional tornadoes.
A sedimentary rock made of angular, broken fragments cemented together — formed by landslides, impacts, or faulting.
The north–south component of the interplanetary magnetic field. When Bz points south (negative), it connects with Earth's field and lets solar energy in — triggering aurora.
Convective Available Potential Energy — a measure of fuel for thunderstorms. Higher CAPE means stronger updrafts and bigger storms.
A massive burst of solar plasma and magnetic field hurled from the Sun. When one hits Earth, it can trigger a geomagnetic storm and widespread aurora.
A gemstone cut with a smooth, rounded top and flat bottom — no facets. 'Cab' for short. Best for opaque or chatoyant stones.
A unit of gem weight: 1 carat = 0.2 grams. Abbreviated 'ct.'
A cast is a copy of a fossil formed when sediment fills a mold (the hollow left when the original dissolved).
The current geologic era — from 66 million years ago to today. The 'age of mammals.'
A pale yellow polish compound used for the final mirror finish on quartz, glass, and agate.
The 'cat's eye' effect — a single bright band of light that slides across a stone as it's turned. Tiger's eye is the best known.
A mineral's tendency to break along flat, smooth planes where the atomic bonds are weak. Mica cleaves into thin sheets.
A sedimentary rock made of rounded pebbles cemented in a finer matrix — an ancient riverbed or beach gravel turned to stone.
Relating to rising warm air and sinking cool air — the engine that drives thunderstorms.
A dark patch on the Sun where the magnetic field opens into space, letting high-speed solar wind escape. A common, steady source of aurora activity.
The typical shape a mineral grows in — prismatic, bladed, tabular, acicular (needle-like), and so on.
The shape and quality of a finished gem — faceted or cabochon. 'Cut' also means the work of shaping a stone.
A NWS alert issued when wildfire smoke reduces visibility enough to make travel hazardous.
A widespread, long-lived wind storm caused by a fast-moving line of thunderstorms. Produces damage along a path hundreds of miles long.
A sticky wax used to attach a gem to a 'dop stick' (a handle) so it can be held during faceting.
The act of attaching a stone to a dop stick with dop wax so it can be precisely oriented for cutting and polishing.
A coating of tiny, sparkling crystals covering a surface or lining a cavity. Often seen on quartz geodes.
A subdivision of a geologic period. Example: the Pleistocene epoch is part of the Quaternary period.
The largest division of geologic time. The three eras of the Phanerozoic are Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic.
The removal and transport of rock and soil by water, wind, ice, or gravity. Sculpt the land surface over time.
A crystal with well-formed, visible faces — it had room to grow into its ideal shape.
An extinct 'sea scorpion' — giant arthropods that lived in ancient oceans. New York's state fossil.
A measure of solar radio flux at 10.7 cm wavelength — a proxy for overall solar activity. Higher values mean more energy available for aurora.
Cutting a transparent gem with many flat, angled faces (facets) to maximize brilliance and fire.
A crack in the Earth's crust where rocks have slipped past each other. Earthquakes happen on faults.
Solar flare strength categories, weakest to strongest: A, B, C, M, X. Each class is 10× the one before it. M and X flares can drive major aurora.
A sudden, dangerous flood — usually within a few hours of heavy rain. Can sweep away vehicles and fill slot canyons.
A glow produced when UV light hits a mineral and it emits visible light instantly. Stops when the UV is removed.
Any preserved trace of ancient life — a bone, shell, footprint, or impression — at least 10,000 years old.
The way a mineral breaks when it doesn't follow cleavage planes. Quartz shows a conchoidal (curved, shell-like) fracture.
A hollow rock lined with crystals inside — usually quartz or calcite. Cut open to reveal the sparkling cavity.
NOAA's 5-level storm scale: G1 minor, G2 moderate, G3 strong, G4 severe, G5 extreme. Higher levels push the aurora oval farther south.
An ancient southern supercontinent that included Africa, South America, India, Antarctica, and Australia.
A coarse, light-colored igneous rock rich in quartz and feldspar. Common in continental crust.
Tiny extinct colonial animals that floated ancient oceans. Their fossils look like saw-blade or pencil marks on rock.
The abrasive powder (silicon carbide, diamond) used on grinding wheels. Measured in mesh — smaller numbers are coarser.
A mineral's resistance to scratching. Measured on the Mohs scale from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).
A measure of spin in the lower atmosphere. High helicity plus high CAPE means a tornado risk.
A hook-shaped radar signature that often marks a tornado-producing supercell.
Relating to hot, mineral-rich water — the source of many ore deposits and crystal pockets. 'Hot water.'
The Sun's magnetic field carried through space by the solar wind. Its orientation (especially the Bz component) controls whether aurora fires.
Rock formed from the cooling and solidifying of magma or lava. Basalt and granite are igneous.
A foreign material trapped inside a crystal as it grew — another mineral, a gas bubble, or water. Often visible in quartz and emerald.
A fossil from a species that lived briefly but widely — used to date the rock layer it's found in.
The upper layer of Earth's atmosphere where solar particles excite atoms and create the glowing aurora.
A rainbow play of color caused by light bending through thin layers. Seen in bornite ('peacock ore') and opal.
A 0–9 scale of geomagnetic disturbance, measured every 3 hours. Kp 5+ means a geomagnetic storm; higher Kp pushes the aurora visible farther south.
A rare fossil site with exceptional preservation — soft tissues, feathers, or complete skeletons. 'Storage place' in German.
Molten rock once it reaches the surface — magma that has erupted from a volcano.
A sedimentary rock made mostly of calcium carbonate — often from accumulated shells and coral. Caves form in it.
How a mineral's surface reflects light — vitreous (glassy), metallic, adamantine, pearly, silky, or earthy.
Molten rock below the Earth's surface. When it erupts, it becomes lava.
The magnetic bubble around Earth that deflects most of the solar wind. Aurora forms where some particles sneak in near the poles.
A metamorphic rock formed from limestone under heat and pressure. Used for sculpture and building.
A event where a large percentage of species die out in a short time. The 'Big Five' mass extinctions shaped life on Earth.
A mineral habit with no visible crystal shape — a compact, shapeless mass.
The rotating updraft inside a supercell thunderstorm — the precursor to most tornadoes.
The era from 252 to 66 million years ago — the 'age of reptiles.' Includes Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods.
Rock changed by heat, pressure, or hot fluids — without fully melting. Marble (from limestone) and schist are metamorphic.
A 1–10 scratch-test scale of mineral hardness: 1 talc, 2 gypsum, 3 calcite, 4 fluorite, 5 apatite, 6 orthoclase, 7 quartz, 8 topaz, 9 corundum, 10 diamond.
The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration — operates the SWPC space-weather monitoring center.
The U.S. National Weather Service — issues watches, warnings, and advisories.
A rounded, lumpy mass of mineral — smaller and more irregular than a geode, often solid throughout.
A volcanic glass — lava cooled so fast no crystals formed. Breaks with sharp, conchoidal fractures.
A slice of oceanic crust and upper mantle thrust up onto land — a window into the deep Earth.
An extinct straight-shelled nautiloid. Fossils are common in Moroccan limestone and often sold polished.
The era from 541 to 252 million years ago — the 'age of ancient life.' Includes Cambrian, Ordovician, and others.
The supercontinent that existed from about 335 to 175 million years ago. All major landmasses were joined together.
A soft, pearl-like sheen on a surface. Talc and muscovite mica can show it.
An extremely coarse-grained igneous rock, often the last bit of magma to crystallize. Produces large crystals of tourmaline, beryl, and feldspar.
A coarse, dark, ultra-mafic igneous rock of the mantle. The source rock of diamonds and peridot.
A subdivision of an era. Example: the Jurassic is a period of the Mesozoic era.
Fossilization where mineral-rich water fills the pores of a bone or wood, turning it to stone over time.
A glow that continues after the UV light is turned off — the mineral keeps releasing stored light energy.
The theory that Earth's crust is broken into moving plates. Their collisions build mountains and volcanoes.
Opal's signature flashing rainbow effect, caused by light diffraction through microscopic silica spheres.
When a crystal shows different colors when viewed from different angles. Tourmaline and tanzanite are strongly pleochroic.
The final, mirror-smooth stage of finishing a gem — done with a very fine compound on a soft pad.
A fine abrasive paste used for the final finish: aluminum oxide (general), cerium oxide (quartz/glass), tin oxide (some stones).
All geologic time before the Cambrian (before 541 million years ago) — most of Earth's history.
The rough-shaped stone before final cutting — the stage between slab and finished cab.
The process by which an organism becomes a fossil — usually requires rapid burial and mineral replacement.
A mineral that has replaced another mineral's crystal shape while keeping the original form. 'False form.'
A frothy volcanic rock so full of gas bubbles it floats on water. Used as an abrasive.
A very hard metamorphic rock formed from sandstone. Doesn't scratch with a knife.
A rush of cold, dry air on the back side of a supercell. Often wraps around the tornado.
A NWS alert for critical fire weather — hot, dry, windy conditions where any spark can explode into a wildfire.
Fossilization where the original material is slowly swapped for a mineral (often silica or pyrite), molecule by molecule.
The endless loop where igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks transform into one another over geologic time.
Unworked, uncut gemstone material as it comes from the ground — the starting point for cutting.
The NOAA center that issues severe thunderstorm and tornado outlooks and watches.
NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center — the source of the Kp forecasts, watches, and warnings this app uses.
A sedimentary rock made of sand grains (mostly quartz) cemented together. Forms cliffs and canyons.
A metamorphic rock with visible, aligned mica or chlorite flakes — gives it a sparkly, layered look.
A dark, vesicular volcanic rock — heavier than pumice and doesn't float.
Rock formed by the accumulation and cementing of sediment — sandstone, shale, limestone. Often holds fossils.
A thunderstorm with winds ≥58 mph, hail ≥1 inch, or a tornado. Triggers a NWS warning.
A fine-grained sedimentary rock made of compacted mud or clay. Splits into thin layers.
Wind that changes speed or direction with height. Strong shear tilts storms and helps them rotate.
A band of rock deformed by intense, sideways-directed pressure. Often hosts gold and other hydrothermal deposits.
A fibrous, silk-like sheen — seen in fibrous gypsum (satin spar) and some asbestos minerals.
A thin slice cut from a rough rock on a trim saw — the first step in making a cabochon.
A sudden, intense flash of light and radiation from the Sun. The biggest flares can trigger aurora a day or two later.
A constant stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. Faster, denser wind means stronger aurora.
A measure of a mineral's density compared to water. Galena feels very heavy; quartz feels 'normal.'
A solid line of thunderstorms out ahead of a cold front. Often produces damaging winds and hail.
The color of a mineral's powder when scraped on an unglazed porcelain plate. Often more reliable than the mineral's surface color.
Where one tectonic plate dives beneath another into the mantle. Produces volcanoes and earthquakes.
A crystal with partial, imperfect faces — somewhere between euhedral (perfect) and anhedral (no faces).
A sudden, explosive brightening and expansion of the aurora — often the most vivid, dancing displays happen during a substorm.
The most powerful thunderstorm type — a long-lived storm with a rotating updraft. Produces the largest hail and strongest tornadoes.
A metal or plastic outline guide used to mark the shape of a cabochon on a slab before cutting.
How a mineral resists bending or breaking — brittle, malleable, sectile (can be cut with a knife), or elastic.
A reversible color change caused by light — hackmanite fades in sunlight and returns in the dark.
A glow produced when a mineral is gently heated. Some fluorite specimens emit light when warmed.
A violently rotating column of air touching the ground. The most intense weather phenomenon on Earth.
Evidence of an animal's activity rather than the animal itself — tracks, burrows, or coprolites (fossil dung).
A flash of light produced when a mineral is scratched, crushed, or rubbed. Some quartz and fluorite specimens show it.
An extinct marine arthropod with a three-lobed body. One of the most iconic and collectible fossils.
A rock made of consolidated volcanic ash. Light, soft, and easy to cut — used as building stone since antiquity.
Polishing rocks in a rotating barrel with progressively finer grits over weeks. Produces smooth, polished pebbles.
Ultraviolet light bands used to make minerals fluoresce: Shortwave (254 nm), Midwave (312 nm), and Longwave (365 nm). Different minerals respond to different bands.
A sheet-like deposit of minerals filling a crack in rock. Quartz and calcite veins are common.
The minimum Kp needed to see aurora from your latitude. Higher (farther south) latitudes need higher Kp.
A glass-like shine — the most common mineral luster. Quartz, fluorite, and olivine all show it.
A lowered, rotating cloud base beneath a supercell — often where a tornado forms.
A NWS alert meaning severe weather is occurring or imminent. Take action now.
A NWS alert meaning conditions are favorable for severe weather in the next few hours. Stay alert.
The breakdown of rock at or near Earth's surface — by water, ice, wind, chemicals, or living things.
val definition: String
